ViTacSim uses a tri-modal tactile primitive: a global sparse contact-force lattice, a local dense force array, and tactile images. Anchored to PhysX contact-solver outputs, it corrects normal inconsistency through local stiffness alignment and reconstructs tangential forces under decoupled slip-stick regimes while preserving GPU parallelism. A joint projection preserves the sparse wrench and enforces local friction cones. ViTacBench spans parallel grippers, dexterous hands, and bimanual systems, with tasks ranging from vision-dominant to tactile-dominant regimes. ViTacPolicy aggregates variable numbers of heterogeneous tactile inputs using spatial-pose embeddings and a Transformer, and aligns force-array and tactile-image modalities through a two-stream VQ-VAE with a shared codebook. Controlled Hertzian-reference indentation and real-sensor sliding tests reduce normal and tangential force RMSE from 2.31 and 1.85 N to 0.42 and 0.53 N, respectively. Throughput reaches 2,482.9 tactile-pipeline FPS at 256 parallel environments. Simulation and real-world experiments show gains on several contact-rich tasks, while low absolute success on tactile-dominant tasks highlights the remaining difficulty of purely tactile control.

title: ROVO: Robust Rotation-Only Visual Odometry for UAVs at Low and Moderate Altitudes
authors: Xiaokai Song, Li Zhang, Xichao Teng, Erting Pan, Yibin Ye, Kun Wang, Leqi Liu, Guangcheng Dai
abstract: Image noise can confound rotation and translation estimates in monocular visual navigation for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) at low and moderate altitudes, where even small perturbations may cause large errors in translation direction. Inspired by angular cues in long-range visual perception, we propose rotation-only visual odometry (ROVO) for monocular aerial imagery. ROVO estimates pairwise rotations from matched images, robustly averages them over overlapping windows, and aligns consecutive windows through shared frames. By retaining only orientation in the trajectory state, it prevents uncertain landmark depth from propagating to later estimates. In trajectory simulation, sliding-window ROVO achieved a mean orientation error just 10.7% as large as that of the conventional SLAM baseline. On real flight data, ROVO achieved rotation accuracy comparable to ORB-SLAM3 and DPVO under the original Bell412 settings. With a narrower FoV or at higher flight altitude, ROVO reduced relative rotation RMSE by 19.7--69.4% compared with the next-best method in each comparison. Code and simulation tools are available at https://github.com/sssxxxkkkk/ROVO.

title: Progressive Reliable Supervision for Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation
authors: Jing Li, Zhe Zhang, Huateng Sun, Yuhui Yang, Wanli Xue, Xu Cheng, Fan Shi, Jianhua Zhang, Qinghua Hu, Shengyong Chen
abstract: Black-Box Universal Domain Adaptation (B$^2$-UniDA) aims to adapt a target model to an unlabeled target domain under arbitrary label-space relationships, while neither source data nor source-model parameters are accessible during adaptation. Under such restrictive information access, reliable target supervision is unavailable, while predictions from the black-box source model can be unreliable due to source bias and domain shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Progressive Reliable Supervision (PReS), which progressively establishes and refines reliable target supervision by coordinating complementary knowledge from the black-box source model, foundation models, and the evolving target model. PReS first identifies reliable known samples by exploiting semantic consistency under diffusion-based perturbations and cross-model consensus between the black-box source model and CLIP. It then estimates the sample-wise reliability of the two predictors and adaptively integrates their complementary predictions to construct reliable pseudo labels. The resulting supervision is exploited asymmetrically to encourage confident and discriminative predictions for reliable known samples while maintaining uncertain yet locally consistent predictions for potential unknown samples. As adaptation proceeds, the emerging target-domain knowledge is further leveraged to refine both the pseudo labels and the known/unknown sample partition, forming a closed-loop process in which supervision construction and target adaptation mutually reinforce each other. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets under diverse label-space relationships demonstrate that PReS achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance under the restrictive B$^2$-UniDA setting.

title: OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution
authors: Zhilu Zhang, Xiaoyu Liu, Wenxi Liu, Shengfeng He
abstract: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

title: Teaching Time Without Losing General Retrieval: Adapting Multimodal Embeddings for Time-Sensitive Video Retrieval
authors: Toya Oyama, Rainer Lienhart, Shin'ichi Satoh
abstract: In text-to-video retrieval, MLLM-based embedding models do well when the text describes the scene (general retrieval), but poorly when it describes actions and their direction (time-sensitive retrieval). TARA, a pioneering work, fine-tunes such a model on text triplets with temporal hard negatives; it improves time-sensitive retrieval but lowers general retrieval (mean R@1 over six benchmarks in our rerun on Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B: 58.4->44.8), and its released model keeps general retrieval only when ensembled with Qwen3-VL-Embedding. Our goal is strong general and time-sensitive retrieval with one model and one vector per clip. Three findings lead to three simple components. Keep loss: general retrieval follows how far the output embeddings drift from the base model, not how far the weights move; we therefore keep them near the base model, which keeps most general retrieval even without general-domain data. Pair loss: the text embeddings of an action description and its reversed-direction version are well separated, but the video embeddings of a clip and its reversed copy are close; we therefore widen the gap between the video embeddings of each clip and its reversed copy, in the direction of the difference between their two text embeddings. Middle-layer LoRA: frames are combined in the middle layers, and temporal information peaks in or just after them; we therefore train LoRA only on these layers, which nearly matches training all weights on most time-sensitive benchmarks with 0.15% of the parameters and keeps general retrieval better. General R@1 stays at 58.4, while R@1 with each clip's reversed copy in the gallery rises from 55.5 to 63.2; the gains carry over to unseen benchmarks and InternVL2-8B-RA. The keep loss is also a remedy for the TARA recipe (general R@1: 44.8->57.8), and ensembling TARA with Ours gives the highest scores on RTime and unseen CiA among the compared models.

title: Multi-Agent Coordination Through Stigmergy for Canal Network Formation on Real Terrain
authors: Jordan Kennedy, Federico Oliva, Amir Degani, Karen-Lee Bar Sinai, Nare Karapetyan
abstract: Terrain-modifying robot swarms operating in unstructured outdoor environments must coordinate under uncertain dynamics despite unreliable communication and incomplete global information. Stigmergy offers a decentralized alternative by allowing agents to coordinate indirectly through persistent environmental modifications, yet its application to large-scale terrain construction on real landscapes remains largely unexplored. Inspired by beaver canal construction, we present a minimal stigmergic framework for multi-agent systems in which decentralized agents follow local wetness cues, excavate terrain, and interact through a closed agent--environmental feedback loop. The framework couples agents with seasonal hydrology on a real digital elevation model (DEM). Across 110 simulations on an 862m x 1167m region spanning agent count and hydrological recession rate, the model produces emergent canal-like networks whose morphology varies predictably with environmental constraints. An alignment-invariant morphological evaluation against a field-annotated reference network identifies parameter regimes that reproduce key canal characteristics, while failure cases reveal over-canalization and fragmentation. These results demonstrate that simple local terrain-modifying behaviors can generate plausible landscape-scale structures through environmental feedback, providing a minimal framework for studying decentralized terrain construction and bio-inspired swarm coordination.

title: Boomerang identities and binomial transform
authors: Bernd C. Kellner
abstract: In Pascal's triangle, the boomerang identities, which were recently introduced, combine and extend the well-known hockey-stick identities of the binomial coefficients by allowing additional terms. We show that the binomial transform of sequences in a ring play a central role in this context. Subsequently, we show several applications to Bell and Bernoulli numbers and polynomials, Appell polynomials, as well as, to harmonic, Fibonacci, Lucas, and Stirling numbers.

title: Benchmarking Evidence Sufficiency in Vision-Language Models for Autonomous Driving
authors: Nhat Ha Nguyen, Sudipta Chowdhury, Lokesh Das
abstract: Reliable driving VLMs must do more than answer correctly or localize relevant scene actors: they must determine whether the available visual evidence is sufficient to support an answer. Existing evaluations largely treat grounding and answerability as separate measurements, making it difficult to distinguish well-supported predictions from those localized to relevant but insufficient evidence. We introduce DriveAnswer, a benchmark of 20,151 questions across seven reasoning families, that operationalizes this distinction using matched strong- and weak-evidence configurations. Each pair preserves the underlying scene fact and semantic answer while changing whether the observations support answering, making abstention the appropriate response under weak evidence. On the six-family evaluation, the strongest zero-shot baseline reaches 67.31% strong-evidence accuracy, yet only 21.55% of matched questions satisfy both answer-abstain behavior and complete grounding. With controlled adaptation, Gemma-4-12B reaches 63.29% on this joint capability, nearly tripling its zero-shot performance. Qwen3-VL-8B exhibits the same broad improvement in evidence-sensitive answering and grounding. These results show that semantic correctness, evidence sufficiency, and grounding are distinct capabilities that should be evaluated jointly.

title: From Historical Schedules to On-Sky Control: Autonomous Scheduling on the 4-m Blanco Telescope
authors: Rachel Hur, Paul Chichura, Alex Drlica-Wagner, Eric H. Neilsen, Guillermo Damke, Aleksandra Ciprijanovic
abstract: The scientific efficiency of ground-based astronomical observatories relies on effective decision-making in a dynamic, multi-timescale environment with complex scientific rewards. Traditional observation schedulers are designed and tuned by domain experts to handle these considerations using heuristic rules based on models of the environment and observational system. Here, we leverage historical data to train an automated telescope scheduler using behavior cloning (BC). The BC scheduler is trained purely on historical datasets; it is not given expert scheduling heuristics nor an optimal scientific reward. It is then evaluated in order of increasing realism: first on expert states, then in closed-loop offline rollouts, and finally during autonomous operation with real-time feedback on the NSF's Victor M.\ Blanco 4-m Telescope. On expert states from holdout nights, the BC policy closely matches the expert distribution over airmass and Moon separation. During closed-loop rollouts on the same nights, we find that the per-observation data-quality metric, $t_{\rm eff}$, falls by $6.9 \pm 3.4\%$ relative to the expert's. During on-sky deployment, the policy scheduled $149$ exposures in $5.2$ hours with an average $t_{\rm eff} = 0.75 \pm 0.26$, consistent with closed-loop rollout evaluations. No additional degradation was observed when transitioning to real observing conditions. This represents the first real-world, real-time deployment of a learned autonomous scheduler on a leadership-class national observatory and establishes a path toward on-sky evaluation of reinforcement-learning-based schedulers trained on archival schedules augmented with counterfactual trajectories.

title: Polynomial-Time Learning of Random Automata from One Label per Word
authors: Yilin Cheng
abstract: We study a binary deterministic finite automaton whose $2n$ transitions are chosen independently and uniformly from its $n$ states. The learner observes independent uniform words of length $m$, each labeled with a single bit indicating acceptance. For every fixed $β>0$ we give a polynomial-time algorithm that works outside a set of transition tables of probability $o(n^{-β})$. On each remaining table, for any start state and accepting set, the predictor has error at most $ε$ on fresh uniform words of length $m$ with probability at least $1-γ$ over the training sample and the learner's random choices. Its sample size and running time are polynomial in $n$, $m$, $1/ε$ and $\log(2/γ)$, with degree depending only on $β$. Although each word reveals only one output, comparing label moments at two consecutive history lengths lets us estimate the expected product of the signed outputs of two continuations from the same hidden state. We also refute Conjecture 4 of Fish and Reyzin on meeting times. For two distinct states fixed before the table is drawn and every fixed $c>0$, the fraction of words of length $\lfloor cn\rfloor$ that send them to different states converges in probability to $e^{-c}$. On a typical table, driving this fraction down to $1/n$ takes asymptotically $n\log n$ letters. Selected proof steps are formalized in Lean.

title: Attestation is All You Need: Toward a Zero-Trust Architecture for HPC AI Agents
authors: Jie Li, Chenxu Niu, Tongyang Wang, Yong Chen
abstract: AI agents are beginning to automate data analysis, orchestration, and simulation steering in HPC environments, but they introduce a security problem that existing cluster defenses do not address: the hijacked authorized agent. An adversary can subvert an agent through prompt injection, poisoned shared data, compromised tools, or multi-agent coordination, then exfiltrate sensitive data through legitimate encrypted LLM API traffic. We propose behavioral attestation as a runtime defense for this setting. Our system, AEGIS, compiles task-derived behavioral constraints, monitors agent actions with ebpf-based syscall interception, verifies evidence against constraint profiles, correlates behavior across agents, and triggers slurm-level containment. On the real attestation path, AEGIS detects all four implemented attack classes with sub-second median latency at a 1-second interval and low measured verifier overhead. Controlled experiments show full attack-suite coverage, stronger detection than representative baselines, and no observed false positives on the evaluated benign workflows.

title: Do Vision-Language Models Know Their Own Visual Weaknesses? Probing Capability-Level Metacognition
authors: Dohoon Kim, Taesup Moon
abstract: Metacognition includes knowing one's own strengths and weaknesses across kinds of tasks, not only judging whether a single answer is correct. We test whether vision-language models (VLMs) know in advance which kinds of visual tasks and image conditions are hard for them, across a wide range of open and proprietary models. Because some tasks are hard for every model, we separate what a model knows about this shared difficulty from what it knows about itself. We find that VLMs know little in advance about their visual weaknesses. They misjudge their overall accuracy and do not even know which kinds of tasks are hard for every model, and most misjudge how degraded images affect them. We further train VLMs to predict their own accuracy, which teaches them their own level of accuracy on kinds unseen in training but not which kinds are hard for them. However, information about these weaknesses appears once a model starts solving. On a few unlabeled questions of a kind, the probability a model assigns to its own answers follows weaknesses particular to the model, across kinds of tasks and image conditions. VLMs thus hold information about their own weaknesses that their stated predictions do not yet reflect. By separating what is particular to a model from what holds for every model, our evaluation offers a test for methods that aim to teach VLMs their own weaknesses, and the answer probability offers them a signal to start from.

title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation
authors: Ayush Barik, Fan Lai, Francis Y. Yan
abstract: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.

title: Reading Decisions Before Spans: Efficient Generative Verification
authors: Yanbin Gong, Lei Chen
abstract: A developer checking an assistant's report may need only an alarm that a claim is unsupported. A generative verifier, however, can continue decoding to quote and classify the errors. We study how much of that output is needed to recover its decision. In a frozen 2B span verifier, the choice between an empty error list and its first object precedes all localization. Native8 stops generation at this branch. The preceding seven syntax tokens are fixed, so Prefill1 supplies them as input and generates only the unrestricted branch token, using the same native instruction. On 2,015 code-agent TEST responses, Prefill1 reduces eager resident service by 84.84% relative to full generation, with released-reference F1 of 83.43 versus 83.41. It saves 31.98% over Native8 even though their logical token totals are identical. Under default compiled execution, the extra saving is 6.74-26.73% on the complete workload, with small decision changes. Controlled evidence interventions and first-location decoding establish what these shorter readouts retain and what requires further generation.

title: Efficient inferential models and their fiducial connections
authors: Max Raner
abstract: Valid inferential models (IMs) provide frequentist calibration guarantees, but validity alone does not determine which construction is most informative. We study finite-sample efficiency through concentration risk, the expected volume under a possibility contour. For a smooth, fully identified association and a specified parameter-volume measure, a weighted Neyman--Pearson argument identifies the generalized fiducial density as the optimal score for minimizing cut volume subject to fixed-data auxiliary compatibility. The resulting maximum-specificity transform gives an explicit volume interpretation of the fiducial efficiency ceiling, which need not itself be sampling valid. We develop two approaches to valid construction. The first minimizes design-averaged concentration risk among single, data-independent auxiliary-compatible contours. The design measure prioritizes efficiency without requiring prior beliefs or restricting validity. The second localizes the parameter-volume score to candidate-specific contours, yielding a normalized, valid IM equivalent to sampling validification of the relative fiducial likelihood. A parallel sample-space construction recovers the ordinary likelihood-ratio IM; direct validification of the ceiling provides another repair. For the same association, exact, data-independent predictive contours share a common fiducial distribution as a saturating inner probability, while generating different calibrated confidence-region geometries. Design averaging thus selects an efficient member without changing the underlying fiducial law. Examples in a two-component measurement model and an exponential scale model illustrate the efficiency gains and show that sampling-valid repair can improve on the raw ceiling by leaving the fixed-data auxiliary-compatible class over which it is optimal.

title: Algorithms and Complexity of Connectivity Switching in Graphs
authors: Christoph Kern, Alexander Firbas, Manuel Sorge
abstract: We study computational problems in switch graphs. A switch graph consists of a vertex set and a set of switches, which are collections of edge sets. The goal is to find a configuration, that is, a selection of one edge set per switch, such that the resulting graph satisfies a desired property. This general framework unifies several switching models from prior work, with applications in solving Boolean equation systems, network routing, and SNP genotyping. We focus on connectivity-related switching problems, such as finding a configuration that yields a connected graph (global connectivity) or that connects a specific pair of vertices (local connectivity), presenting polynomial-time algorithms and establishing NP-completeness results depending on the switch structure. For local connectivity, we obtain a full complexity dichotomy. Furthermore, we introduce a natural weighted variant and analyze its parameterized complexity, proving W[1]-hardness with respect to the solution weight via reductions from restricted variants of the weighted satisfiability problem (WSAT). As a byproduct, we resolve an open question of Kanj and Szeider (TCS 2015) on the parameterized complexity of a specific WSAT variant.

title: Sharp Casorati Inequalities for Pointwise Bi-Slant Riemannian Maps into Sasakian Space Forms
authors: Tanveer Fatima
abstract: We establish Casorati inequalities for pointwise bi-slant Riemannian maps into Sasakian space forms with the characteristic vector field tangent to the range. The Sasakian structure imposes specific conditions on the second fundamental form, leading to refined inequalities for the normalized horizontal scalar curvature that also account for O'Neill's tensor. For proper pointwise bi-slant maps, equality in the two principal inequalities is characterized by the vanishing of the second fundamental form on the orthogonal complement of the characteristic direction in the range. We also derive corresponding inequalities for pointwise semi-slant, hemi-slant, and slant Riemannian maps and construct examples attaining equality.

title: KuroANN: Avoiding Unnecessary SSD Reads in High-Recall Filtered Vector Search
authors: Soobin Cho, Nakyung Lee, Jiwoong Park, Gyuyeong Kim
abstract: We present KuroANN, a new on-SSD filtered vector search system for partition indexes. Existing solutions assign the same number of SSD reads to all queries within a given selectivity range, wasting I/O for many queries. KuroANN instead assigns each query's SSD reads based on the number of vectors that pass its filter, called its match count. This is based on our observation that the match count is known before the search and that the number of SSD reads a query requires depends on this match count. KuroANN measures offline how many partitions to probe and candidates to read for the target recall at each count. At runtime, a query looks up these numbers, filters only the probed partitions, and stops reading from the SSD when further reads are unlikely to help. This significantly avoids unnecessary SSD reads and filtering work, improving throughput and latency at high recall. Experimental results show that KuroANN outperforms PipeANN-Filter and Faiss by up to 34.5x and 9.10x, respectively.

title: Dirac Propagation for Simulating Fermionic Observables under Particle-Number-Conserving Unitaries
authors: G Arnav Naidu, Matteo D'Anna, Adrián Pérez-Salinas, Jannes Nys, Juan Carrasquilla
abstract: Simulating the dynamics of interacting fermions remains a central computational challenge across physics and chemistry. We introduce Dirac propagation, a classical method that simulates local observables in fermionic systems subject to particle-number-conserving unitaries. We show that, in the operator expansion, strings with weights above the total particle number can be discarded without incurring any error in the final expectation value. This exact cutoff bounds the number of retained strings polynomially in the number of modes at fixed particle number, including for interacting dynamics. The formalism combines a compact representation with explicit expressions for interacting gates and exact treatment of number-conserving fermionic Gaussian and Clifford unitaries. This framework offers an approach to simulating fermionic many-body dynamics and classically benchmarking fermionic quantum circuits.

title: Motion Conditioned World Modeling for Embodied Visual Tracking
authors: Jiahao Zhang, Xuan Yao, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
abstract: World models support embodied decision-making by predicting future environment states. In embodied visual tracking, uncertain target motion and robot-induced viewpoint changes jointly affect visual observations, making future-state prediction challenging. We propose Motion-Conditioned World Modeling, which incorporates predicted target-motion distributions and robot ego-motion into latent state transitions. A Geometry--Progress module jointly models geometric paths and single-step travel distances through shared motion modes and path-conditioned progress distributions. This formulation captures uncertainty in route selection and motion progress while preserving their dependence. Action-induced coordinate transformations express predicted paths in the next robot frame, providing geometrically grounded conditions for future visual-state prediction. Future visual feature reconstruction supervises the motion predictor through the conditioned transition branch, linking explicit motion representations to subsequent observations. The model is jointly optimized with motion likelihood, feature reconstruction, and expert-action supervision, enabling the tracking policy to combine visual context with predictive motion cues.Experiments on three embodied tracking benchmarks demonstrate improved tracking performance and cross-environment generalization with a lightweight $0.5$B backbone.

title: A Dimension-Free Bound on the FDR of the Benjamini-Hochberg Procedure under Slowly Decaying Gaussian Correlations
authors: Zuofeng Shang, Wenge Guo
abstract: The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure is proven to control the false discovery rate under independence and under positive dependence. Under arbitrary dependence, however, its guarantee deteriorates by a factor that grows logarithmically with the number of hypotheses. For Gaussian test statistics, it is unknown whether dependence can make the false discovery rate grow with the number of tests. We study this question when the correlation between two test statistics decays with the distance between their indices. We seek guarantees that hold uniformly over a wide class of correlation structures and over all configurations of the signals. We show that if the correlations decay at least as fast as a power of the inverse logarithm of the distance with exponent larger than one, then the false discovery rate of the original BH procedure is bounded by the nominal level times a factor that does not depend on the number of hypotheses. This factor grows only polylogarithmically as the level decreases. The result holds for both one- and two-sided tests, and the procedure uses no knowledge of the correlations. The class allows correlations of both signs. The required decay can be arbitrarily close to the inverse logarithm. The key technical tool is a truncated Hermite expansion of the exceedance indicators. It shows that their main fluctuations are common to all thresholds that BH may use. These fluctuations can be well controlled, while the remainder is too small to accumulate, which leads to a bound that does not inflate with the dimension.

title: Discretely self-similar solutions to coupled fluid systems with locally $L^2$ data
authors: Chen-Chih Lai, Tai-Peng Tsai
abstract: In this paper we present a systematic way to construct discretely self-similar solutions of fluid systems, including the viscous resistive magnetohydrodynamics equations, the viscoelastic Navier-Stokes equations with damping, and the Oberbeck-Boussinesq system, for locally $L^2$ initial data which are not necessarily in the uniformly local $L^2$ space. The solutions satisfy local energy inequalities, local a priori bounds depending only on the $L^2$ norm of the initial data in a fixed ball (and, for the Oberbeck--Boussinesq system, on the force), and a limiting formula for the pressure.

title: Biomechanically Grounded Prediction of Selective Motor Control and Clinical Outcomes from Infant Video
authors: Divya Joshi, Ruize Yang, Colleen Peyton, R. James Cotton
abstract: Early identification of cerebral palsy (CP) relies on observational assessments of spontaneous infant movement, such as the General Movement Assessment (GMA) and the Baby Observational Selective Control AppRaisal (BabyOSCAR), which require trained raters and substantial scoring time. Existing automated approaches derive hand-engineered features from two-dimensional keypoints, which describe image-plane motion rather than the three-dimensional behavior of individual joints. We present Baby Biomechanical 3D Body (BB3D), an infant-adapted, biomechanical pipeline that estimates joint-angle trajectories from single-camera video. Against a multi-view markerless motion capture reference in 17 infants, BB3D's median Procrustes-aligned error was 17.5~mm for joint centers and 20.4~mm for marker sites. A spatio-temporal transformer, pretrained on BB3D joint-angle trajectories from 1k+ single-camera recordings, and fine-tuned on 550 videos from 350 infants, predicted each individual BabyOSCAR item with a mean within-site AUC of 0.79 and the BabyOSCAR total with a Spearman correlation of 0.86 on held-out recordings. Without being trained on diagnosis, the predicted total separated infants with CP from those without CP with an AUC of 0.86, exceeding a replicated two-dimensional feature classifier (0.67) but below the expert clinician rater's total (0.97). Predicted scores also carried information about functional ability and body distribution, though less than expert clinician scores. These results show that biomechanically grounded representations of monocular video can support scalable, joint-level assessment of selective motor control in infancy

title: Convexification effects of $L_p$-sums
authors: Matthieu Fradelizi, Auttawich Manui, Mark Meyer, Maud Szusterman, Artem Zvavitch
abstract: It is a classical result, quantified by Shapley, Folkman, and Starr, that the Minkowski averages of any compact set asymptotically approach its convex hull in the Hausdorff metric. In this paper, we investigate the analogous convexification phenomenon for the Firey $L_p$-sums of compact sets. First, we establish new structural properties of the $L_p$-sum. Notably, we show that the iterated $L_p$-sum of compact sets whose convex hull contains the origin is eventually starlike. We then study $L_p$-convexification for three classical measures of nonconvexity: Hausdorff metric, volume deficit, and effective standard deviation. For each of these measures, we prove that the $k$-fold $L_p$-sum averages of a compact set $A$ converge to $\text{conv}(0,A)$ when $1<p<\infty$, and to $\text{conv}(A)$ when $p=\infty$. In each case, we show that the convergence to the convex hull is eventually monotone. For the Hausdorff metric and effective standard deviation, we prove sharp upper bounds for the $L_p$-sum of two compact sets.

title: What Does a Skill Vocabulary Cost? A Closed-Loop Decomposition over Demonstrated Motions
authors: Maximilian Xiling Li, Nils Blank, Paul Mattes, Pankhuri Vanjani, Rudolf Lioutikov
abstract: Discrete skill policies execute motions drawn from a finite vocabulary. In most current methods, this vocabulary is a latent codebook learned jointly with a selector and a decoder. When such a policy fails in closed loop, the failure cannot be traced to the vocabulary, to the choice of skill or to its execution. We present Movement Prototype Quantization (MPQ), which places a library of demonstrated motions after a trained policy instead of inside it. MPQ replaces each predicted action chunk with its nearest library element, corrects that element toward the prediction within a bound, and trains no parameters. Across six architectures, including a 7B vision-language-action model, the wrapped policy is statistically equivalent to the original. A reference policy executed through the library is therefore a baseline for any selector over the same library. Substituting a selector's components one at a time attributes its shortfall to them. On LIBERO-90, with selectors on three backbones, quantization costs nothing and the choice of skill costs at most 2 points under the reference's placement and correction. The selectors' own placement and correction account for nearly all of the remaining gap, up to 12 points. Offline reconstruction predicts none of these differences and misjudges library size, design and transfer across benchmark suites. Project page: https://intuitive-robots.github.io/mpq.

title: Modified recombination or dynamical dark energy (or both)?
authors: Alexander Reeves, Gabriel P. Lynch, Andrina Nicola, Jens Chluba, Alexandre Refregier
abstract: Several recent analyses report a hint of modified recombination when the latest cosmic microwave background (CMB) and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data are jointly analysed. We examine whether this preference persists when allowing for departures in the late-time expansion history of the Universe. We fit a seven-parameter reconstruction of the free-electron fraction and a $w_0w_a$ dark-energy model, separately and jointly, to DESI DR2 BAO, a $5\times2$pt combination of galaxy clustering and CMB lensing, and three CMB likelihoods: P-ACT, Planck PR4 and Planck 2018. With a cosmological constant, our baseline data combination favours early recombination near last scattering, agreeing with previous analyses. Allowing for dynamical dark energy (DDE) removes this preference, while the constraints on $w_0$ and $w_a$ change little when the recombination history is marginalised over. DDE has the lowest Akaike information criterion of the models we consider for every data combination, and adding recombination freedom to it raises the AIC by $5.1$--$11.7$ and is disfavoured by the Bayesian evidence. We interpret these results in terms of CMB predictions for the BAO distances: earlier recombination and DDE both shift these predictions towards the measurements, but only DDE also changes the redshift dependence of the late-time expansion, which anisotropic BAO measurements constrain. We support these conclusions using noiseless mock data, finding that fitting modified recombination to a mock Universe generated with DDE reproduces the apparent preference for modified recombination, whereas DDE cannot similarly reproduce the signatures of modified recombination. The preference for modified recombination found with a cosmological constant therefore reflects the discrepancy between the CMB and BAO, rather than independent evidence for departures from standard recombination physics.

title: MINDS: The mid-infrared spectrum of the disk, jets, and winds of DG Tau
authors: Manuel Güdel, Péter Ábrahám, Till Kaeufer, Ágnes Kóspál, József Varga, Nicole Pawellek, Kamber Schwarz, Valentin Christiaens, Danny Gasman, Matthias Samland, Ewine F. van Dishoeck, Thomas Henning, Aditya M. Arabhavi, Alessio Caratti o Garatti, Pacôme Estève, Adrian Glauser, Göran Olofsson, Benoît Tabone, Göran Östlin
abstract: DG Tau is one of the best-studied young stellar objects in transition from a Class I protostar to a T Tauri star. It is no longer embedded in a dense molecular cloud, but still reveals features that are commonly seen in protostars at earlier evolutionary stages. DG Tau hosts a protoplanetary disk and two energetic jets that can be studied down to the immediate environment of the star and disk at optical, infrared, and X-ray wavelengths. We use the Medium Resolution Spectrometer of MIRI on the James Webb Space Telescope. DG Tau's mid-infrared spectrum consists of a very bright continuum with various silicate features, and lines of CO, H$_2$O, OH, H I, H$_2$, Ne$^{+}$, Ne$^{2+}$, Ar$^{+}$, Fe$^{+}$, and Ni$^{+}$. We find substantial grain growth to at least 2 $μ$m at an early evolutionary stage. Lines of H$_2$O and CO are formed at extremely high temperatures (600-2000 K). The ratio of warm to hot water is the lowest among previous observations of disks with JWST. This and a very strong continuum point toward the relevance of the strong accretion of DG Tau and consequently strong stellar UV irradiation. The pair of jets reveals a rich spectrum of emission lines from ions, in particular producing forbidden lines of [Ne II], [Ne III], [Ar II], [Fe II], and [Ni II]. The forward jet shows a collimated structure as found previously, while the hitherto poorly described, receding jet is more widely dispersed on scales of several arcsec, showing a layered structure with the fastest components being the most collimated. The ionization of the jet gas cannot be reconciled with high-energy radiation from the star itself. Instead, we propose a unified nonequilibrium ionization shock model in which the previously studied X-ray jet plasma continuously cools, recombining ions until, at temperatures around $10^4$ K and below, metals at low ionization stages emit the observed ion lines.

title: Strong hyperbolicity of puncture-gauge formulations of gravitational theories with second order equations of motion
authors: Shunhui Yao
abstract: We prove that the modified CCZ4 (mCCZ4) formulation, used in nonlinear puncture-gauge simulations of (d+1)-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity and four-derivative scalar-tensor theory in four dimensions, is strongly hyperbolic for both theories at sufficiently weak coupling, provided that the gauge parameters are chosen to satisfy a cone-separation condition. The proof applies to the full principal symbol of the theories, extending previous analyses based on first-order perturbation theory about the Einstein limit. We establish strong hyperbolicity by recasting the mCCZ4 equations into a formally equivalent second-order system whose derivative structure resembles that of the modified harmonic formulation of Kovács and Reall. This allows us to adapt their covariant characteristic analysis and continuity argument, without assuming that individual eigenvalues or eigenvectors depend analytically on the coupling. We also show that standard CCZ4 in general relativity is strongly hyperbolic in puncture gauge away from two defective degeneracies.

title: ab-indices for lattice path matroids
authors: Cenk Aydin, Giovanni Caiolo, Chiara Giardino, Mara Gruß, Mikael Häglund, Elena Hoster, Christian Stump
abstract: The base polytopes of connected lattice path matroids admit subdivisions into snakes. We use these to obtain an explicit positive combinatorial description of their ab-indices, their Chow polynomials and their chain polynomials. We finally apply this description to the particular case of the ab-index of Schubert matroids.

title: Field Life: Particle Life as Interacting Chemical Fields
authors: Iliya Zhechev
abstract: Field Life is a cellular automaton inspired by the interaction dynamics of Particle Life. In Particle Life, each particle has a colour, and an interaction matrix sets how strongly each colour attracts or repels each other colour. In Field Life, each colour is a channel of the automaton, and each cell holds a concentration of every colour. One step of the rule has three parts. Each colour is convolved with a ring-shaped kernel, which measures how much of that colour surrounds a cell. The interaction matrix combines these measurements into an attraction for each colour. The mass of each colour then moves toward higher attraction, in a way that conserves mass. A random matrix and a random initial state are usually enough to produce moving structure: bodies that glide, bodies that shed diffuse clouds, and gliders that break up into smaller gliders. We sample rules at random, keep the rules that move and form structure, and describe the patterns that appear: colours that sort into regions, colours that form stripes, and gliders, compact bodies that travel across the grid. The simulation and 120 saved rules, which we call worlds, are released.

title: Recipe for near-unity efficient frequency conversion via transient molecular modulation
authors: Arturo Mena, Pau Arcos, María Sánchez-Hernández, Amaia Berganza, Joseba Zubia, David Novoa
abstract: Frequency transduction technologies are an essential element for interfacing devices operating at distinct spectral regions. Specifically, the conversion of weak signals between different wavelengths is a fundamental requirement of quantum networks, where conversion efficiency is critical for preserving the statistical properties of light. In this regard, molecular modulation in gas-filled hollow-core fibers offers a promising approach for highly-tunable linear frequency conversion of classical and quantum light. However, recent experimental studies in this subject have struggled to overcome a saturation in conversion efficiency to about 70%, which, although high, might impair the faithful transfer of quantum properties upon conversion. In this work, we discuss a route to surpass this limitation that identifies the key factors to consider for obtaining quantum efficiencies exceeding 99%. These results might pave the way to viable fiber-based quantum transduction schemes for next-generation quantum networks.

title: Quantization-Induced Performance Degradation in Segment Routing: A Concentration Inequality Analysis
authors: Kai Wang, Chee Wei Tan
abstract: In segment routing (SR), splitting ratios must be quantized to respect practical hardware precision constraints. Yet no existing work has established an upper bound on the performance degradation caused by such quantization. In this work, we propose source-agnostic systematic rounding, which allows flows sharing a destination to share the same policy, thereby reducing memory consumption, and which approximates the target splitting ratios by a set of power-of-two terms so as to respect the hardware precision limit. We explicitly analyze the consequence of quantizing splitting ratios to integer multiples of 1/64 by a probability-theoretic argument based on concentration inequalities, and we derive an upper bound on the resulting performance degradation. We validate our analysis with extensive experiments on real-world network topologies and flow statistics.

title: Patterson-Sullivan Theory for Approximate Groups
authors: Isaac Weaver
abstract: In this paper we consider the limit set of a uniformly discrete approximate subgroup acting on a negatively curved manifold, and prove several properties comparable to that of the classical case of discrete groups, including a version of the dichotomy between elementary and non-elementary groups. Furthermore, we adapt the Patterson-Sullivan construction for discrete groups to obtain asymptotic counting results for the orbits of infinite uniformly discrete approximate groups acting on a negatively curved manifold.

title: Normative and neural network models of multisensory integration
authors: Marcus Ghosh, John S. Butler
abstract: Animals continuously detect scents, sights and sounds, which their brains combine into diverse multisensory streams. Multisensory integration accelerates learning, increases reaction speeds and helps to resolve sensory ambiguities. In studying this process, the field has developed a continuum of models; from concise mathematical equations, with a handful of variables, to artificial neural networks, with billions of parameters. In this review, we divide this spectrum into two classes: normative models start from a hypothesis about how multisensory signals should be integrated, while neural network models aim to emulate how circuits could integrate them. Together, these models demonstrate that observers can integrate cues in a statistically optimal fashion, and help to explain experimental findings, including the diversity of multisensory neuron response profiles and network architectures. In this review, we provide a didactic overview of multisensory models, complete with accessible equations and Python code, and compare their assumptions and explanatory power. We detail what has been learned from these models. Finally, we discuss how the ideas and insights from classical theoretical models can be reconciled with those from artificial neural networks, and how this convergence should shape future research.

title: Breaking the Joint Action Space Dependence in Distributionally Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yue Wang
abstract: We study the sample complexity of learning robust coarse correlated equilibria (CCE) in finite-horizon, general-sum, distributionally robust Markov games with known rewards and a generative model of the nominal transitions. Each player evaluates a policy by its worst-case return over total-variation (TV) balls centered at the nominal transition distribution of every stage, state, and joint action; this is the standard $(s,a)$-rectangular uncertainty set. Existing generative-model guarantees for this model scale with the number $\prod_iA_i$ of joint actions, where $A_i$ is the number of actions of player~$i$. Since this number grows exponentially with the number of players, these guarantees suffer from the curse of multiagency. We design an algorithm whose sample complexity depends on the action sets only through the largest individual action-set size $A_*:=\max_iA_i$. The algorithm uses $\widetilde O(SA_*H^5D^4/\varepsilon^4)$ transition samples and, with probability at least $1-δ$, returns a Markov policy that is an $\varepsilon$-robust CCE from every initial state. Here $S$ is the number of states, $H$ is the horizon, and $D:=\max_i\min\{H,1/ρ_i\}$, where $ρ_i$ is the TV radius of player~$i$. Two ingredients make this possible: a plug-in estimate of the robust backup whose mean error does not depend on the number of states, and a single batch of samples per round that serves as bandit feedback for all players at once. The result shows that the dependence on $\prod_iA_i$ can be avoided without modifying the $(s,a)$-rectangular uncertainty set.

title: The Alma catalog of OB stars. IV. A massive star census of the Magellanic Clouds System
authors: J. A. Molina-Calzada, J. Maíz Apellániz, M. Pantaleoni González
abstract: Context. The Magellanic Clouds System (MCS), comprising the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (LMC and SMC) and the Magellanic Bridge (MB), offers a nearby laboratory for studying massive stars. Existing catalogs are limited by extinction, crowding, and incomplete cross-validation with the literature. Aims. We identify candidate stars with initial masses of roughly 8 solar masses or more, including O- and early-B-type stars, supergiants, luminous blue variables, and Wolf-Rayet stars. We aim to improve completeness in reddened and crowded regions and recover sources missed by large surveys. Methods. We combine Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry with SIMBAD, HST, and complementary optical and infrared surveys. We select candidates using color-magnitude and color-color diagrams, extinction tracks, Gaia astrometry and variability, and spectral classifications. We check for duplicates and multiple systems, include literature and HST-resolved sources without reliable Gaia counterparts, especially in 30 Dor, and derive synthetic Gaia photometry where Gaia measurements are incomplete. Results. ALS IV contains 51 954 massive star candidates: 36 506 in the LMC, 15 264 in the SMC, and 184 in the MB. It provides homogeneous identifiers and coordinates, multiwavelength photometry, astrometry, variability diagnostics, and spectral classifications where available. Complementary photometry and HST observations recover reddened and crowded sources missed by Gaia-based selections. The sample traces the main massive-star populations and prominent star-forming regions across the MCS. Conclusions. ALS IV provides the most comprehensive census of massive star candidates in the MCS and serves as a reference for massive-star studies and future surveys and Gaia releases.

title: The integer group determinants for the abelian groups of order 27
authors: Michael J. Mossinghoff, Chris Pinner
abstract: We completely determine the integer group determinants for $\mathbb Z_3 \times \mathbb Z_9$ by resolving the allowable multiples of $3$. This completes the Taussky-Todd integer group determinant problem for the abelian groups of order $27$.

title: Toward Solving the Galactic Foreground Problem in Gravitational-Wave Astronomy with Machine Learning
authors: Bo Liang, Jinwen Deng, Minghui Du, Hanlin Song, Xilong Fan, Peng Xu, Ziren Luo, Lijing Shao
abstract: Space-borne gravitational-wave detectors will see tens of millions of Galactic binaries. Resolved, they would form a census of the Galaxy's ultracompact binaries unhindered by dust; unresolved, they are the dominant noise up to a few millihertz for massive black-hole binaries, extreme-mass-ratio inspirals and backgrounds from the early Universe. Separating the two requires the number of binaries, which is ill-defined because binaries exist at every amplitude. We make it an observable by defining a source as a binary above a signal-to-noise threshold. Neural flows count the binaries to within one in 99% of 1 microhertz intervals over 0.5-10 mHz, and nested sampling resolves them, even pairs closer than one frequency bin. The data themselves set a limit: a source is resolvable only if its signal pays for its own description, about 20 nats, which biases even ideal trans-dimensional samplers. Like the diffraction limit in imaging, this Bayesian confusion limit is set by the data rather than by the method, and it governs any superposition of weak sources, from radio surveys and pulsar timing arrays to super-resolution microscopy. For future space-borne detectors, the method turns the Galactic foreground into a definite, calibrated count of binaries with an analytic selection function, the basis for global fits and for tests of population models.

title: Embodied Intelligence for Spectrum Map Construction in Low-Altitude Wireless Networks
authors: Hongtao Liang, Yiyao Wan, Jiahuan Ji, Lingda Meng, Fuhui Zhou, Qihui Wu
abstract: Accurate spectrum map construction by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) is crucial for intelligent resource management in low-altitude wireless networks (LAWNs). Although various construction approaches have been investigated, their performance often degrades under extremely sparse sampling because purely data-driven models may not capture the underlying propagation physics. To address these challenges, an embodied intelligence framework is proposed, which synergistically integrates closed-loop perception-cognition-execution (PCE) coupling and embodied exploration to achieve precise and efficient spectrum construction. Based on this framework, a corresponding embodied cognition and decision network (ECDNet) with three tightly coupled modules is designed. Specifically, by leveraging distance-aware convolutions, the semantic bridge, and adaptive feature alignment mechanisms, ECDNet establishes the bidirectional information flow between construction and decision-making. Simulation results show that ECDNet achieves a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.787 dBm at 4.00% sampling under the non-revisiting spiral protocol. Furthermore, a practical UAV-based spectrum construction platform is developed and field-deployed to provide prototype-level evidence that the sensing, cognition, and action modules execute as a closed loop on size, weight, and power constrained UAV edge devices.

title: Accuracy of Noise Ceiling Estimators for Brain Scores
authors: Aude Maier, Lucas Gruaz, Martin Schrimpf, Johanni Brea
abstract: The internal activations of modern machine learning models align surprisingly well with the activities recorded in real brains. In the last five years, the alignment between encoding models and brain activities, often called brain scores, has steadily increased. Because brain recordings are noisy, there exists an upper bound to the brain scores that any model can achieve. This bound, called the noise ceiling, is crucial for two reasons: it determines whether further improvements in model performance are possible, and it enables meaningful comparisons of brain scores across benchmarks. The field has developed multiple approaches to estimate noise ceilings, but the statistical properties of existing estimators remain poorly understood, leaving it unclear in which experimental settings they provide reliable estimates. Here, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for brain recordings, use it to derive closed-form expressions for four commonly used noise ceiling estimators, and provide theoretical predictions for the behavior of each estimator. We validate the theoretical predictions with simulations that we compare to noise ceiling estimates in existing fMRI and EEG datasets. We find that the existing methods underestimate the true noise ceiling in different settings. We conclude with recommendations for best practice in different situations.

title: Keypose or Dense? A Controlled Comparison of Action Representations for Stage-Structured Manipulation
authors: Haizhou Ge, Mengshuo Wang, Zhixing Chen, Lei Han, Chen Wang, Lu Shi, Guyue Zhou, Ruqi Huang
abstract: Most imitation policies that predict chunks of future actions use the dense action representation, in which the chunk holds one control target per step. In stage-structured manipulation, where a task can be divided into stages with definable endpoints, the keypose action representation instead sets each step of the chunk to the endpoint of the stage that step belongs to, and a speed-capped servo supplies the motion. We compare the two in several simulated manipulation tasks and on a real robot, with the same chunk length and matched demonstrations, observations, policy architectures and update budgets; in simulation, each one's execution rule is selected on tuning scenes. When the simulated demonstrations are slowed, paused and rerouted, dense success falls sharply while keypose stays roughly level, across three policy architectures and with endpoints extracted from the recorded demonstrations; keypose also leads under object-size and position shift. With clean demonstrations, keypose leads only when they are scarce and is otherwise close to or behind dense across the simulated tasks, provided that the demonstrations and execution rule suit its executor; when they do not, it falls far below dense. The same dependence on the executor appeared on a real robot learning to open a drawer from human demonstrations: dense succeeded more often, and keypose improved substantially only after its executor's rotation and forward speed were adjusted to the demonstrations. These results suggest that keypose trades sensitivity to such variation in the demonstrations for sensitivity to execution that departs from them.

title: Measuring Layer-wise Intrinsic Dimensionality of FFNs in LLMs via PCA
authors: Daehee Kim
abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) keep the feed-forward network (FFN) intermediate width identical across every layer, a convention inherited from the original Transformer. Yet mechanistic work suggests layers at different depths do qualitatively different work, raising a natural question: are their capacity demands also non-uniform, and if so, can a fixed parameter budget be allocated more wisely than uniformly? To probe this, we apply principal component analysis (PCA) to the input of each FFN down-projection and measure, for every layer, its intrinsic dimensionality as the smallest number of principal components needed to reconstruct the activation up to a fixed cosine similarity. Scanning 58 open-weight LLMs spanning 14 families and 70M to 72B parameters, we find a recurring middle-heavy profile in which middle layers carry higher intrinsic dimensionality than edge layers; the profile is robust to the calibration corpus, even across English and Chinese, and is largely preserved through post-training fine-tuning. As a direct test that this signal is structurally meaningful, we use it to guide width pruning in a knowledge-distilled student under a matched parameter budget: the PCA-guided allocation outperforms the uniform-width convention by +2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and +2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B, while lower-dispersion teachers show smaller gaps (+0.9 on Gemma-3-4B, +0.5 on LLaMA-3-8B), and a budget-matched inverted control does worst on all four teachers. Across these four teachers, the size of the gap tracks how unevenly the teacher's intrinsic dimensionality is distributed across layers (a single-number summary we call $σ_{99}$), and the advantage persists through downstream supervised fine-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/lidf.

title: C3H: Compression-to-Consensus Criteria Hijacking in Multimodal LLM Recommender Systems
authors: Guowei Guan, Yurong Hao, Jiaming Zhang, Fuyao Zhang, Wei Yang Bryan Lim
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are transforming recommender systems into content-aware decision systems. In these systems, multimodal compression and cross-modal fusion are often viewed as robustness-enhancing mechanisms against content manipulation, as compression can filter noisy signals and cross-modal consensus can suppress inconsistent anomalies. We challenge this assumption by showing that the same process can expose a compression-to-consensus (C2C) bias in ranking decisions. Signals that remain salient after compression and receive consistent support across modalities can gain disproportionate influence in candidate comparison, offering an exploitable direction for content manipulation. In this paper, we introduce C3H, a novel inference-time attack that exploits this vulnerability. Rather than relying on noisy perturbations or training-time poisoning, C3H promotes a target item by tailoring its multimodal content to align with the decision criteria implicitly expressed by the recommender. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C3H substantially increases target-item exposure while maintaining overall recommendation utility. Code is available at https://github.com/GuoweiGuan666/C3H.

title: Beyond Fixed-Context Likelihood: Zero-Shot AI-Generated Text Detection via Context Perturbation Discrepancy
authors: Yifan Tang, Jingran Li, Yihao Wang, Zhen Yang, Jianyi Liu, Gongshen Liu, Ru Zhang
abstract: The same increase in token log probability from earlier context can be typical at one position and unusually large at another. We introduce Context Perturbation Discrepancy (CPD), a zero-shot detector that measures this gain relative to what a single pretrained language model expects. Keeping the passage fixed, CPD scores each observed token under its full prefix and under a short window of recent tokens. Under the full-prefix distribution, the expected gain equals the KL divergence from that distribution to the restricted-prefix distribution. CPD subtracts this expectation from each observed gain and scales the sum of the signed deviations by its analytical reference standard deviation. On unedited human and AI texts from GEN, DetectRL-X, and HART, subtracting the expected gain raises AUROC by 32.78-35.81 percentage points at the same variance scale. CPD outperforms seven zero-shot baselines, averaging 94.80% AUROC and 79.60% recall at a 5% false-positive rate. On original and edited HART passages, the same scores separate texts more clearly by draft origin than by the benchmark's final-expression labels (89.15% versus 65.50% AUROC). Code is available at https://github.com/BUPT-tyf/CPD.

title: Contract2Reach: Discretization-Induced Contractive Dynamic Programming for High-Dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability
authors: Jaeyoung Lee, Donggun Lee, Jason J. Choi, Namhoon Cho
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) enable undiscounted Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis for high-dimensional systems, but their performance can be sensitive to hyperparameter choices and the underlying system dynamics. We introduce Contract2Reach, which recasts undiscounted finite-horizon reachability as a sequence of contractive fixed-point problems solved by backward time marching. Our formulation combines discretized temporal and spatial derivatives to construct a contractive mapping without introducing a discount factor. Under standard assumptions, we prove that the exact scheme converges to the unique viscosity solution as both the temporal and spatial step sizes tend to zero. Unlike PINNs, our training fits rollout-based value targets via a single regression, without backpropagating through spatial value gradients. In the neural implementation, adaptive zero-level-set sampling and conservative target combination address high-dimensional sample sparsity and false positives, respectively. Experiments on a parameterized vertical drone, a 13D quadrotor, and a 40D publisher-subscriber system show competitive performance against PINNs-based baselines. Boundary evaluations on the vertical drone and publisher-subscriber systems demonstrate improved fidelity and reduced learning-rate sensitivity, revealing errors that volume-based metrics can miss.

title: Lattice Thermal Conductivity of MgO and the MgSiO$_3$ Polymorphs Bridgmanite and Post-Perovskite at Lower-Mantle Conditions Using Fine-Tuned MACE Potentials
authors: Amrendra Kumar Tiwari, Sandro Jahn
abstract: Heat flow across the core-mantle boundary (CMB) depends on the lattice thermal conductivity ($κ_{\mathrm{latt}}$) of lowermost-mantle minerals, yet calculated CMB values for MgO differ severalfold, and high-temperature estimates of the conductivity increase across the bridgmanite-post-perovskite transition range from about 20 to 50%. Direct solutions of the linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation (LBTE) require thousands of density functional theory (DFT) force evaluations per thermodynamic state. Here we replace these evaluations with phase-specific, fine-tuned MACE potentials for MgO, MgSiO3 bridgmanite (Pv), and MgSiO3 post-perovskite (PPv). The potentials reproduce DFT energies, forces, stresses, pressure-volume relations, and compressed-state phonons for all three phases. For MgO at 0 GPa, replacing MACE forces with DFT forces in otherwise identical transport calculations changes $κ_{\mathrm{latt}}$ by 0.2% at 300 K and 1.9% at 2000 K. PPv is 44-55% more conductive than Pv at the same pressure and temperature and strongly anisotropic, with $κ_{[100]}/κ_{[010]}$ ranging from 1.7 to 2.1. The quasi-harmonic phase boundary has a Clapeyron slope of $(7.4 \pm 0.1)$ MPa/K and intersects a model geotherm at 116.2 GPa and 2660 K, where the transition raises the silicate conductivity by 47%, to 8.6 W/(m K). Heating in the basal thermal boundary layer lowers the MgO and PPv conductivities to 37.3 and 6.7 W/(m K) at the CMB, where Hashin-Shtrikman bounds of 9.5-11.4 W/(m K) for an Fe-free aggregate of 80 vol% silicate and 20 vol% MgO encompass the 10 W/(m K) used in earlier heat-flow estimates. The density-temperature parameterizations provide an intrinsic end-member reference for lower-mantle thermal models.

title: Elliptic Monotonicity Formulas for $p$-Green Functions
authors: Yu-Zhao Wang
abstract: In this paper, we derive $p$-Laplace analogues of Colding's three monotonicity formulas in the original metric on complete noncompact $n$-dimensional manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature, for $n\geq3$ and $1<p<n$. We assume a normalized positive minimal $p$-Green function vanishing at infinity with Euclidean pole asymptotics. Two complementary linearizations and the $p$-Bochner formula yield exact derivative identities with a common nonnegative defect involving an anisotropic trace-free Hessian and Ricci curvature. These identities give exterior cone rigidity and integral defect estimates, and recover the sharp gradient estimate and Euclidean rigidity of Mari--Rigoli--Setti. A one-parameter extension of Colding--Minicozzi type connects the formulas with known monotonicity and convexity identities for $p$-capacitary potentials.

title: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models
authors: Wonjune Seo, Minkyung Park, Saerom Park
abstract: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.

title: Multiscale Zoom-in Lattice Simulation for Inflation
authors: Xinpeng Wang, Angelo Caravano, Leander Thiele, Misao Sasaki
abstract: Lattice simulations are a powerful tool for studying the nonlinear evolution of inflationary fluctuations. The exponential expansion, however, makes it challenging to cover a broad range of scales relevant for the dynamics, limiting how many e-folds a single fixed grid can follow. We develop a three-dimensional zoom-in lattice method to follow inflationary fluctuations over a broad range of scales from the adiabatic subhorizon regime through horizon crossing. Every few e-folds, the grid is refined into one or more subgrids, with small-scale power injected and large-scale fluctuations inherited from previous generations. Each zoom shifts the resolved band while keeping its dynamic range fixed. This extends the duration over which lattice simulations can follow inflationary fluctuations from a few e-folds to tens of e-folds. In a Starobinsky benchmark evolved for 50 e-folds, the curvature power spectrum agrees with linear theory. In a model with an oscillatory feature, the zoom-in simulations recover the peak seen in a high-resolution fixed-grid run and show scale-dependent non-Gaussianity.

title: Why wait? Optimal rules for intertemporal decisions across life history, economics and machine learning
authors: Elias Tannira, Luís M. A. Bettencourt
abstract: When should we take a smaller reward now rather than wait for a larger one later? This question recurs across evolutionary biology, behavioral ecology, psychology, economics and artificial intelligence, yet each field treats temporal discounting differently. We show that intertemporal decisions across these disciplines share a common structure and a single optimal rule: wait while the growth rate of the reward exceeds the discount rate, and act when the two rates become equal. For a single decision, this rule defines an optimal waiting time; for a continuous reward stream, it becomes an equation of motion for quantities apportioned over time, such as consumption or fertility. We derive reward and discount rates from explicit mechanisms, including mortality and other hazards, uncertainty and risk aversion, population growth, capital depreciation, dread, subsistence thresholds and the value of information, with examples from laboratory choice, retirement, maturation, resource extraction, capital accumulation and exploration. The framework shows how apparent anomalies, including hyperbolic discounting, the sign effect and the impatience of deprivation, can arise from the relative structure of rewards and hazards rather than from fixed preferences. Finally, we identify what must be measured to explain and modify temporal preferences in experiments and policy.

title: Convex computation of cost bounds for data-driven nonlinear optimal control
authors: Oumayma Khattabi, Matteo Tacchi-Benard, Sorin Olaru
abstract: The paper addresses the optimal control problem of an input-affine polynomial system with an unknown (state-dependent) input matrix affecting the control effectiveness. Under assumptions on the existence of a data set and the Lipschitz continuity of the unknown part {of the dynamics}, an uncertainty set is constructed and used to adapt the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation towards a data-driven formulation. We solve it for the best-case scenario, thus giving a lower bound on the best cost achievable by means of a feedback control policy. After relaxing it into a moment-SoS hierarchy of semidefinite programs, a control law is extracted from the primal on moments and compared with other benchmark methods in a numerical application.

title: Lattice models of chiral random motion: A short review
authors: E. Kalz, J. Wojcik, N. Sherf, Y. Roichman, R. Metzler
abstract: Chirality, a systematic rotational bias, is ubiquitous in many random motion patterns, from bacteria cells, that swim in circles near surfaces and spinning colloids, to charged particles diffusing under the influence of magnetic fields. In two dimensions, chirality renders random transport \textit{odd}: the diffusion tensor acquires an antisymmetric part that leaves the mean-squared displacement invariant but modifies fluxes and boundary currents. Lattice models for random motion are a natural setting to study chirality, since they are exactly solvable, connect directly to heterogeneous media, cellular automata, and programmable robots, and in discrete time admit fully chiral limits with a localised bulk and edge transport. Lattice walks with a rotational bias have been introduced in different communities several times since 1960, yet without a common language or conceptual connection between them. Here we review these models from the perspective that on the lattice, chirality requires memory. Taking the recently introduced chiral random walk model as a template, we describe the walker with an internal degree of freedom. With a chiral biased updating rule, the full diffusion tensor of this chiral walker turns odd. Within this picture, we can unite persistent and chiral walks, run-and-tumble motion, and cyclic random motions in one framework. We discuss how the memory is followed into the environment; in Lorentz lattice gases, kinetic and rotor walks, and random odd environments; and into the path; in spiral self-avoiding walks.

title: What it is to Obey
authors: Mark Whitmeyer
abstract: Prior to agents taking part in a simultaneous-move game, a designer commits a device that sends signals to each of the agents, evaluating the resulting set of equilibria according to a (Hausdorff-)continuous function. In games of incomplete information I show that it must be without loss of optimality for the designer to restrict attention to direct obedient devices if and only if she assumes her preferred equilibrium will be played. In games of complete information, I characterize the monotone evaluations, which include both the maximally optimistic one and the maximally pessimistic one.

title: Qwen-Image-HD: Autoregressive Diffusion for High Definition Image Generation
authors: Zihao Liu, Zekai Zhang, Shengming Yin, Zikai Zhou, Donghao Zhou, Chenyang Zhu, Lihan Jiang, Ningyuan Tang, Bingxuan Zhao, Yanran Zhang, Yan Shu, Zhening Liu, Jiahao Li, Jie Zhang, Kaiyuan Gao, Kun Yan, Qihang Ai, Rui Song, Shuo Cao, Xiao Xu, Xiaoyue Chen, Yuxiang Chen, Zhendong Wang, Zhouyang Li, Bo Zheng, Jun Zhou, Xiu Li, Chenfei Wu
abstract: Fine-tuning a generator on a complete high-resolution canvas requires long image sequences and substantial computation, yet local regions can still exhibit unnatural repetitive stripes when training resources are limited. We introduce Qwen-Image-HD, which adapts Qwen-Image 2.0 to high-resolution synthesis through local training and blockwise autoregressive generation. Each prediction covers a target tile at 1K scale, conditioned on high-resolution upper and left neighbors and a compressed historical thumbnail. These conditions provide adjacent fine-scale structures and an overview of the scene generated so far. To integrate these complementary cues, we map both forms of history and the target to a shared canvas coordinate system to express their spatial relationships and scale differences. On Qwen-Image-Bench at 4K, Qwen-Image-HD achieves stronger overall evaluation performance than direct 4K generation with FLUX-3-Image-Klein. Compared with full-image 4K supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone, it achieves better generation quality with lower training compute and higher inference efficiency, while exhibiting fewer unnatural repetitive stripes in original-resolution comparisons. We further introduce a Wavefront-AutoRegressive inference schedule that generates tiles on the same anti-diagonal concurrently across GPUs to reduce single-image latency.

title: A degree-sum condition for paths through prescribed vertices
authors: Kun Cheng, Leilei Zhang
abstract: Let $G$ be a graph of order $n$ and let $S\subseteq V(G)$. Denote by $κ(S)$ the minimum size of a vertex set separating two vertices of $S$, and by $σ_p(S)$ the minimum degree sum over all independent sets of $p$ vertices in $S$. We prove that if $κ(S)\ge k\ge2$ and $σ_p(S)\ge n+(p-1)^2$ for every integer $p\ge k$, then any two distinct vertices of $S$ are joined by a path containing all vertices of $S$. This gives a path version of Ota's theorem on cycles containing a prescribed set of vertices. As an application, we prove a conjecture of Faudree, Faudree, Gould, Jacobson and Magnant: for $k\ge3$, every $k$-connected graph $G$ of order $n$ satisfying $δ(G)>(n+k^2-2k)/k$ and $δ(G)\geα(G)+k-2$ is hamiltonian-connected.

title: Robust inverse dielectric design of skin phantoms for implantable wireless link evaluation
authors: Andreas Prokscha, Ali Alhaj Abbas, Samar Elmaadawy, Mandana Jalali, Yamen Zantah, Josep M. Jornet, Daniel Erni, Thomas Kaiser
abstract: Skin phantoms support reproducible evaluation of implantable wireless links, yet published complex permittivities of skin predict different propagation losses. We formulate a robust inverse design to determine a homogeneous phantom permittivity that minimizes the largest channel-loss difference across selected skin reference models, incidence angles and both transverse-electric and transverse-magnetic polarizations. Computed candidates and analytical lower bounds bracket the optimal mismatch and constrain the critical depth. Across seven frequencies from 5 to 500 GHz, the minimax mismatch at 1.3 mm ranges from 1.13 to 13.72 dB. For a 3 dB tolerance, suitable permittivities exist at every investigated depth at 5 GHz, while critical depths at the other frequencies range from 0.23 to 1.01 mm. Only one of seven material cases from the literature meets a 6 dB tolerance at 1.3 mm. These results translate channel-loss tolerances into quantitative design criteria for skin phantoms used in implantable wireless link evaluation.

title: AG-WAM: Attention-Guided World Action Model for Accurate and Efficient Robot Manipulation
authors: Hongcheng Zhang, Lei Sun, Songxuan Liu, Tengteng Pan, Yuqiang Zhai, Xianglong Xu, Jianya Guo, Xiao Song
abstract: Recently developed World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions, providing predictive context for control. However, existing WAMs typically learn implicit attention allocation with limited explicit action-relevant attention guidance, leading to limited performance. To unleash strong capabilities of WAMs, we introduce explicit attention guidance as a unifying principle and propose our Attention-Guided WAM (AG-WAM), an end-to-end framework with three plug-and-play attention guidance modules that directly reformulate internal attention paradigm in WAMs: the Content-Adaptive Predictive Attention module, the Guidance-Point Visual Attention module, and the State-Conditioned Text Attention module.
